paras: The 1888 Globe jail raid was a failed attempt by six masked men to break into the county jail at Globe, Arizona Territory, early on April 13, 1888, and take out two prisoners, Thomas Burns and Harry Blevins. The men fled when the prisoners raised a cry, and no one was hurt. Outside papers reported it as a foiled lynching, while the local paper said it was unknown whether the raiders meant to lynch or free the prisoners.

Burns and Blevins were held in the Gila County jail at Globe awaiting trial, and Burns was also serving a sentence from the previous term of court. The coverage gives no race for either man and does not say what the charge against them was until after their trial.

According to the Arizona Silver Belt of Globe, someone knocked at the outer corridor door at 2:30 on Friday morning, and when night watchman Hugh Blevins asked whether it was the sheriff, George Shute, a voice answered, "Yes, let me in." Six masked men armed with Winchesters entered, forced the watchman into the inner corridor, and put a guard over him. The others removed one of the two locks on the cage but had trouble with the second, and the prisoners' cries frightened them off. A Globe dispatch printed in Los Angeles put the time at about 1 o'clock and said the men had woken and held up the night jailer.

No arrest of the raiders appears in the coverage, though Burns and Blevins claimed to have recognized three or four of them. About two weeks later Sheriff Shute took the two prisoners to Phoenix for trial after they obtained a change of venue to Maricopa County. In late May Shute reported that both men had been acquitted on a charge of conspiracy, and Burns was left in Maricopa custody to finish his sentence.

The Los Angeles Daily Herald ran the Globe dispatch on April 14 under the headline "Lynchers Foiled," saying the men meant to take out and lynch the prisoners, "it is supposed." The same day the Arizona Silver Belt headlined its account "An Attempted Jail Delivery" and described every theory of the motive as "mere suppositions." Later in April the Mohave County Miner and the St. Johns Herald each ran a one-sentence territorial item that stated the lynching purpose without qualification and gave the first prisoner's name as "Barnes."

The purpose of the raid is uncertain: the dispatch and territorial briefs called it a lynching attempt, but the Silver Belt, the closest source, said it was not known whether the men meant to lynch or release the prisoners, and that the lynching account came from the prisoners themselves.

reader.title: 1888 Globe jail raid
bases: A band of six masked men broke into the Gila County jail at Globe to take out two prisoners, reportedly to lynch them, and fled when the prisoners cried out (A1, A2, A3).

No one was killed: six masked men tried to open the jail cage but fled before reaching the prisoners (A1, A2); the local paper said it was not known whether they meant to lynch or release the prisoners, and no motive was reported (A2).

The Globe dispatch (A1) and the local Arizona Silver Belt (A2), which differ in wording and detail, agree on six masked men, a removed lock and the prisoners' cries; territorial briefs repeat the story (A3, A4).

accounts.label: Globe dispatch
accounts.gist: About 1 a.m. six masked men woke and held up the night jailer and removed one lock, supposedly to take out and lynch the two prisoners, but fled when the prisoners cried out.

accounts.label: Local paper (Arizona Silver Belt)
accounts.gist: At 2:30 a.m. Friday six masked men with Winchesters got in by answering as the sheriff; whether they meant to lynch or release the prisoners was not known, though the prisoners said they recognized some of the men and that they meant to lynch them.

accounts.label: Prisoners' claim
accounts.gist: Burns and Blevins claimed to have recognized three or four of the raiders and asserted that the men intended to lynch them.

accounts.label: Territorial briefs
accounts.gist: On the morning of the 13th six masked men tried to take out Barnes and Blevens and lynch them and were scared off by the prisoners' cries.

framing.detail: The Los Angeles Herald ran the Globe dispatch under 'Lynchers Foiled', presenting the lynching aim as supposition ('it is supposed').
The Arizona Silver Belt headlined 'An Attempted Jail Delivery' and called every theory of the motive 'mere suppositions'.
Territorial papers ran a one-sentence item stating the lynching purpose as fact.
